summary: Defines SNMP managed objects for the X.25 Packet Layer, extending the Internet MIB for managing X.25 networks.

eli5.summary: A list of readings for the part of X.25 that handles calls and data packets, so a monitoring program can check it.

subtitle: The SNMP objects a network manager uses to configure, watch and troubleshoot the packet layer of an X.25 interface.

tldr.problem: X.25 equipment needed a standard way for SNMP managers to configure and monitor the X.25 packet layer, alongside the link layer and the physical line below it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module with seven tables under the x25 object: administrative settings, operating values, statistics, channel ranges, circuits, abnormally cleared circuits and call parameters, plus two traps.
tldr.outcome: Together with the LAPB and RS-232-like MIBs it lets an X.25 stack be managed. It is a Proposed Standard, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.

today: RFC 1382 is a Proposed Standard from November 1992, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this X.25 Packet Layer MIB module.

sections.title: What This MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 1382 defines objects for managing the Packet Layer of X.25 within the Internet-standard Network Management Framework. That framework gives the rules for defining objects (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212), the core objects themselves (MIB-II, RFC 1213) and the protocol for manipulating them (SNMP, RFC 1157).

The abstract says that these objects, along with the LAPB MIB (RFC 1381) and the MIB for RS-232-like hardware devices (RFC 1317), combine to allow management of an X.25 protocol stack. The memo notes that its objects are similar to those in a draft ISO document for X.25 management, which minimizes the instrumentation needed by systems that support both OSI and TCP/IP management.
sections.eli5: This paper lists the readings and switches for one layer of an X.25 connection, so a manager can check on it from far away.

sections.title: How the Layers Show Up in the MIB
sections.content:
A system with a complete X.25 stack over a synchronous line has at least two interfaces in the MIB-II ifTable: one for LAPB and one for the X.25 packet layer. Each software interface names the layer below it. The object x25OperDataLinkId picks the LAPB interface under the X.25 one, and the LAPB object lapbOperPortId picks the synchronous line under LAPB.

Each X.25 subnetwork gets its own ifTable entries, so a system with two X.25 lines has two entries for the packet layers and two for LAPB. The relationship between an X.25 Packet Layer interface and an interface in the Internet-standard MIB is one-to-one, so the ifIndex value directly identifies the matching instances of the objects defined here. Such interfaces have an ifType of ddn-x25(4) or rfc887-x25(5).
sections.eli5: The layers are like stacked boxes, and each box has a label that says which box sits under it, so the manager can follow the chain down to the wire.

sections.title: The Seven Tables
sections.content:
All objects hang under x25, defined as { transmission 5 }. They form seven tables.

  • x25AdmnTable: parameters the administrator reads and sets, used at initialization.
  • x25OperTable: read-only values currently in use by a running interface.
  • x25StatTable: read-only counters of events at the interface.
  • x25ChannelTable: how channel numbers are divided up.
  • x25CircuitTable: information about existing circuits, from calls placed or answered and from PVCs.
  • x25ClearedCircuitTable: termination details of circuits that cleared abnormally.
  • x25CallParmTable: the call parameters used to call other systems, referenced by other tables.

The memo also adds one new data type, X121Address, an octet string of 0 to 17 bytes where each octet holds one ASCII digit of the address.
sections.eli5: Think of seven notice boards: one for settings, one for what is really happening now, one for counts, one for channel numbers, one for open calls, one for calls that ended badly, and one for call recipes.

sections.title: Using the Tables Together
sections.content:
The administrator first sets starting parameters in x25AdmnTable, including a reference to the default call parameters in x25CallParmTable. When the interface is initialized, those values are copied into the interface and can be read back in x25OperTable. Setting ifAdminStatus to up may start the interface. Changing an administrative value may not change the running value until the interface restarts. Timers use the X.25 names, such as the T20 restart timer and the T21 call timer, in milliseconds.

PVCs can be configured in x25CircuitTable before initialization. After that the packet layer adds entries for calls placed or answered. When a circuit clears, its status becomes closed, and if the clear was abnormal an entry is also written to x25ClearedCircuitTable. A closed entry may be deleted by the agent and is always reused when the channel number is reallocated. When resources run short, agents delete the oldest cleared-circuit entry, but must always keep the last one added.

There is no mechanism in this MIB to tell the packet layer to place a call; that belongs in the MIBs of the higher-layer entities that use X.25.

Two traps are defined: x25Restart when the packet layer sends or receives a restart packet, and x25Reset when it sends or receives a reset.
sections.eli5: You write your plan on the settings board, the device copies it to the live board when it starts, and finished calls are tidied up or reused later.

sections.title: Conformance Rules
sections.content:
All the objects are mandatory, and to claim conformance an implementation must support all of them. Some objects relate to optional X.25 features, and for those the MIB defines values that mean the feature is not supported. The agent must still allow reading the object, return that value, and reject set requests that try to change it.

When an optional feature has several objects (window rotation has a timer, a count and a counter for timer runouts), any one object indicating non-support is enough, and the values of the other objects for that feature are undefined. Support of the whole x25 subtree is mandatory for agents of systems that implement X.25.
sections.eli5: Every device must have every dial, but if it does not offer a feature, the dial must read a special value for off and refuse to be turned.

sections.title: Revision History Appendix
sections.content:
An appendix records changes from April 1991 through July 1992 drafts. Examples include changing the index objects of tables that mirror the ifTable to ifIndexType, adding the x25CallParmRefCount object, and changing the range of x25ChannelLIC and x25ChannelHIC from (0..4096) to (0..4095).

The reference count matters in practice: a call-parameter entry can be written only while its reference count is zero, so parameters in use by another table cannot be changed underneath it.
sections.eli5: The back pages list every fix made while the paper was being written, like a change log.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC contains a Security Considerations section of a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It offers no guidance on protecting the writable objects that configure an X.25 interface.
sections.eli5: The paper says nothing about locking the dashboard, so someone else has to think about that.
